How to read this page

Each frame is one surface in one state at one viewport. The grey gutter is outside the page; the white area is the browser viewport at that size. The red dashed rule is the fold — content below it needs a scroll. Frames wider than your window scroll horizontally inside their own gutter; the page itself never does.

Everything inside a frame is rustdoc's own markup and rustdoc's own classes. Every dashed or captioned box — like this — is mock chrome, and is never a style these pages would ship. The surfaces introduce no CSS and no JavaScript at all (UX-012); the only reason this page has a stylesheet of its own is to draw the frames around them.

Two things are simulated rather than rendered, and both are labelled in the stylesheet: a frame's sidebar height (position:sticky;height:100vh cannot mean anything inside a fixed-size stage) and the narrow-700 state (a media query reads the browser viewport, not a 700px-wide div, so the declarations are transplanted verbatim from @media (max-width:700px)).

Two consequences of putting 41 replicas of one page in one document, both deliberate. Heading anchors are namespaced per frame, so «back to the working version» and «start at step one» land in their own frame and can be clicked and judged. #main-content, #rustdoc-toc and #copy-path are not namespaced and therefore repeat: rustdoc styles them by id, and renaming them would ship exactly the unstyled control this stage exists to catch. Links that would leave the page in the real render — ADR-0006, ES-25, the example source — are href="#" here; they carry their real link styling and go nowhere.

What this mock found

Seven things the written design could not have caught, because each one only exists once the real stylesheet and the real API are in the room. None is a matter of taste; each names a decision the approver now has to make.

F-1 — the code column is narrower than the density budget assumes, and the type is bigger

_design.md § Density budget records code at 14px / 21px, citing code{font-size:0.875rem}. That rule is .item-info code. There is no font-size on pre or on .docblock code anywhere in rustdoc-17e0aaed.css; normalize-9960930a.css sets code,kbd,pre,samp{font-size:1em}, so a fence renders at the inherited 16px / 24px.

Two widths were also missed in the chain: .content{margin:0.25em 0.5em} (16px) and .docblock{margin-left:var(--docblock-indent)} (24px). Recomputed, the fence interior is 892px at 1440×900 and 696px at 1024×768, which at Source Code Pro's 0.6em advance is 92 and 72 columns. The binding figure is 72, not the 84 the budget sets, and the 24-line height budget becomes 604px of fence rather than 532px.

Decide: re-cut the budget to 72×24, or accept that every fence scrolls at 1024×768. The overflow-fence frame carries a ruler so the number can be read off the render rather than argued.

F-2 — long headings truncate, they do not wrap, and 11 of 16 headings are over budget

Anti-pattern 5 reads «a sidebar table-of-contents entry that wraps onto a second line», and the Long label state says a heading over 22 characters «wraps to two lines». It cannot: .sidebar-elems .block li a{white-space:nowrap;text-overflow:ellipsis;overflow:hidden}. The entry ellipsizes. As written, anti-pattern 5 can never fire, which makes it a decorative check.

The 22-character figure is also derived from «16px Fira Sans», but .sidebar{font-size:0.875rem} — the TOC is 14px. The threshold is therefore further out than 22 and the failure is silent truncation rather than a visible wrap.

Meanwhile every heading the design names is over 22 characters except three. Look at the sidebar in any frame and read what survives.

F-3 — the payoff line is 93 characters of Debug

println!("{refused:?}") on Result<SequencePosition, AppendError<MemoryStoreError>> renders as one 93-character line. It scrolls at every viewport, and the word the whole project turns on — ConditionViolated — is buried inside a nested tuple struct.

Decide: {refused:#?}, or a shaped line such as println!("the store refused: {refused:?}") preceded by a match, or accept the scroll. The design's own IQ-7 — the refusal is observable, not narrated — is satisfied either way; legibility is not.

F-4 — the fence cannot reach 24 lines, and hiding cannot save it

Written against the API this tree actually has, the refusal program is 31 rendered lines. The transience policy forbids hiding any line that constructs the boundary or observes its refusal, and permits the use block only where it was shown visibly earlier on the same page — which on the crate root it was not. Exactly one line (Ok(())) is eligible. The hidden-line-audit frame shows the arithmetic: 30 lines, not 24.

Decide: raise the height budget, shrink the scenario (the design's own last resort: «the scenario shrinks, not the boundary»), or split step three — which the three-step ceiling forbids.

F-5 — the binding fence in § Signatures calls two things that do not exist

store.head(&seats): EventStore::head takes no argument (crates/happenstance-core/src/store.rs:248). Guard::new(seats, upto): Guard is a #[non_exhaustive] struct with public fields and no constructor (crates/happenstance-core/src/append.rs:130-141), and AppendCondition::new takes a Query, not a list of guards (:146). The verified spelling is read_decision_model(&store, &query) then AppendCondition::new(query).after_opt(last_seen), which is what every fence in this mock uses.

The design does hedge this — the spellings are «the implementer's to take from the merged lib.rs» — but the shape is what is binding, and the real shape is one line longer per boundary, which is part of F-4.

F-6 — the wrong-side contrast asserts the wrong outcome

DT-6 specifies «an AppendCondition whose guard query matches on type only … and it asserts the append is accepted», citing CF-7. But CF-7's named wrong implementation is one that drops the tag join, and the clause says what that costs: it «rejects every command touching any course» (spec/SPECIFICATION.md:7288). A type-only guard is broader than a tagged one, so it over-refuses. It can never be the fence that gets accepted.

The mock therefore draws the wrong guard that really does under-refuse: one tagged with the event being written (course + student) where the invariant spans the course alone. Another student's seat never matches the guard, nothing refuses, and the course goes over capacity. It is still one expression different from the correct fence, it still compiles and runs, and it still asserts accepted.is_ok().

Decide: adopt this framing, or restate DT-6 against the over-rejection failure — in which case the fence asserts ConditionViolated on a write that should have succeeded, and the «outcome the reader should fear» changes from silent corruption to total unavailability.

F-7 — three of the four surfaces have no substrate to be drawn on

opening-encounter, conceptual-bridge and worked-example-handoff are drawn inside rustdoc's chrome because that is the only render shape this repository has. Their routes are {tree}/… and their selectors are honest about reaching only the rustdoc shape. If HS-P0020 pins a different renderer, the three frames' chrome is wrong and only their composition survives — which is what the design says, and this mock is the picture of that risk.
